text.p: Flagship industrial metal copper powered higher on Friday as speculators capitalised on a short-term supply shortage to push the metal to a three-week peak.
At the height of the morning buying spree on the London Metal Exchange (LME), copper for delivery in three months was going for $1,990 a tonne, $46 more than at Thursday's close.
But gains were pared in the afternoon as some investors cashed in profits.
Copper ended the week on the London Metal Exchange (LME) at $1,957, up $13 from Thursday and compared to an opening price of $1,880 on Monday.
The rally boosted sentiment, which was dented early this week when many industrial metals sagged to new recent lows.
"We expect the screws to tighten further," one LME floor trader said, referring to continuing healthy falls in inventories held in LME warehouses after a decline of 9,300 tonnes on Friday.
Tighter nearby supplies have led to cash copper demanding a premium over future material for the first time since September 13.
Traders on Friday were offering up to $8 a tonne more for copper for immediate delivery than for the benchmark three months material.
A week ago the situation was the opposite -- three months metal was up to $13 more expensive than cash copper.

But among other industrial metals, nickel tumbled lower during afternoon ring and kerb trading, against a background of Canadian producer Inco reaching a tentative pay agreement with workers at its Manitoba facilities which could end a two-week lock-out.
Meanwhile, nickel stocks continue to climb, with LME inventories rising another 624 tonnes today. Three months prices sagged back to $7,200 before ending the day at $7,210, down $130 from Thursday.
In the precious metals sector, gold once again threatened to break below the key $380 floor. It held for the time being, but the future looked precarious.
"There was been no sign of real buying so far today at $380.00. In fact, if anything gold is looking a little top heavy," one dealer said.
Gold's latest price fall began on Thursday after investment funds disillusioned by the market's lack of progress compared with booming stock and bond markets, began to sell.

CBOT nearby wheat contracts closed higher on short covering and position squaring before the release Monday of USDA's quarterly grain and oilseed stocks report, traders said. An average of analysts' estimates ahead of the report pegged the U.S. wheat supply as of September 1 at 1.767 billion bushels, below 1.881 billion a year ago.

Traders also said wheat was in a seasonal upswing after sliding recently amid a slowdown in exports and increased competition for export business from other producers. Also, wheat has been forming a technical base, a technician said.
Wheat closed 2-1/4 cents per bushel higher to 2-1/2 lower, with December up 2-1/4 at $4.31-1/2.

NYMEX gasoline prices ended sharply higher Friday after the oil complex shook off earlier profit-taking, but volume was light due to a lack of news. October gasoline settled up 1.61 cents to 64.60 cents a gallon. Traders were selling heating oil - which has risen more than 25 percent in the last three months - to buy gasoline, perceived as having bottomed after recent heavy selling, dealers said. November crude settled 44 cents up at $24.60 a barrel, taking direction from heat and gasoline on a lack of news.

CSCE world sugar futures continued to rack up losses, closing near the day's lows for the fourth consecutive session which saw the most-active March contract fall to its lowest level in three and a half months.

Technically-driven fund selling pushed March to a low of 10.60 and below a previous low of 10.65 made September 12, dealers said. Producer buying on the close buoyed prices off the lows, with March ended at 10.67, off 0.16, having ranged from 10.88 to 10.60.
In London, white sugar futures moved lower during the late afternoon as the earlier fully steady price structure was weakened by a sell-off in the New York raws market, which had opened higher.
The sudden trend reversal prompted fairly widespread liquidation in both markets which resulted in London running up a turnover of 4,805 lots.
Near December traded down to $324.00 a tonne from an earlier high of $328.60. Last business at $324.90, down $2.20 from Thursday. Other active months were between $4.40 and $2.30 down.
In physicals, the only news was Syria filling its requirement for one 13,000 tonnes cargo each of raw and white sugar. Paris white sugar closed with December down $3.30 a tonne at $324.70 a tonne.
